Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking

\setrunningauthor

Li et al.

Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference
with Exact State Forking

Bobo Li1 Affiliation: 1National University of Singapore  2University of Oxford    Jiajia Song1 Affiliation: 1National University of Singapore  2University of Oxford    Hao Fei2 Affiliation: 1National University of Singapore  2University of Oxford    Wynne Hsu1 Affiliation: 1National University of Singapore  2University of Oxford    Mong Li Lee1 Affiliation: 1National University of Singapore  2University of Oxford Affiliation: {libobo, jjiasong, dcshsuw, dcsleeml}@nus.edu.sg  haofei7419@gmail.com Affiliation:  Project Page: https://flide.org Affiliation:  Source Code: https://github.com/OmniJev/flide
Abstract

Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

keywords
Decision Models, Efficient Inference, Prefix Sharing, Hybrid Models, State Forking, Deterministic Inference, Jev

1 Introduction

Large language models increasingly serve as core decision engines within complex systems for tasks such as routing requests (Ong et al., 2024), evaluating responses (Zheng et al., 2023), and deciding the next steps of agents (Yao et al., 2023). Generating text to make categorical choices wastes computational resources on unnecessary tokens and increases latency, leading to the emergence of Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and other specialized decision models (StartLux, 2026; Open-Jev, 2026) for these tasks. These models typically process extensive context, such as a lengthy conversation or an agent trajectory, to answer several questions about it, outputting probability distributions over multiple discrete choices. When deployed on every routed request and agent action, with strict thresholds acting on their probabilities (Decision Index, 2026), these confidence-sensitive models call for an inference engine that is both fast and precise.

However, current inference engines severely constrain the application of decision models since they are optimized for text generation, where the fundamental unit of work is a single linear sequence. When processing decisions, frameworks like vLLM (vLLM Project, 2026d) and SGLang (SGLang Project, 2026c) treat every question as an independent prompt, rendering, tokenizing and scheduling the shared context once for every question. The latest vLLM computes the shared context of a request once before its questions (vLLM Project, 2026b), yet every question still runs as a sequence of its own and resumes from the prefix cache. On hybrid architectures this cache restores recurrent states only at block boundaries (Pan et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2026), and every question and every agent step thus computes the tokens past the last boundary again. Alternatively, multi-item scoring (SGLang Project, 2026a) appends all questions to a single context with a delimiter token before each. Every question then reads this extra token, which changes its hidden states and corrupts its output probabilities compared to isolated prompts (SGLang Project, 2026b). Furthermore, under dynamic batching, the order of floating-point sums changes with the batch (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), which can yield fluctuating decisions for the identical request under varying server loads. All of these issues severely compromise the reliability and efficiency of decision model serving.

The root cause is a mismatch between the logical structure of a decision request and the physical structure in which current engines execute it. Logically, the questions of a request are separate branches of a tree whose trunk is the shared state, and each branch must see only the trunk and itself. Physically, these branches should run together over a single copy of the trunk, which speeds up inference by computing the trunk only once and letting many short branches fill the GPU in one pass. Generation engines tie the physical layout to the logical one, running every question as a separate sequence that computes or reloads the trunk again. Multi-item scoring ties them the other way and does run the branches together. Yet it writes the tree into the sequence itself, and its delimiter tokens enter the input of every branch and, as Figure 1 illustrates, shift the probabilities and flip decisions. Closing this gap means running the branches together while each still computes exactly what it would compute alone, so the physical stream must keep apart the branches it places side by side. An attention layer can keep them apart with a mask, yet the Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2025) of hybrid models such as Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) fold every earlier token into one recurrent state, through which a branch would inherit its siblings. Separating the branches there requires each of them to restart from the exact state of its trunk, inside the same pass that computes the trunk.

To address this, we propose Flide (Flat-Graph Inference for Decision Models), an efficient and exact inference engine that separates the logical structure of decision requests from their physical execution on the GPU. Flide lays a round of requests out as one flat token stream and records their dependencies in GPU-resident metadata. With ForkAttention, the attention and Gated DeltaNet layers follow these dependencies, and in exact arithmetic every question computes what it would compute alone. Since the request structure is encoded in data, a small set of recorded execution graphs can serve different request compositions. The same state-forking mechanism also supports growing agent histories, allowing later requests to resume from checkpoints saved during earlier inference passes. In addition, an optional batch-invariant mode fixes floating-point reduction orders to keep answers bitwise identical across server loads.

We evaluate Flide against state-of-the-art inference engines on workloads ranging from one question per passage to articles and agent trajectories with many questions. Experimental results show that Flide answers up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang on public hybrid models and leads on dedicated decision models. Its throughput leads at every concurrency level whenever a shared state carries several questions. Meanwhile, as multi-item scoring shifts probabilities to gain throughput, Flide yields outputs closest to the float32 reference distributions in total variation distance. These results establish that separating the logical structure of decision requests from their physical execution lets an inference engine be exact and fast at once.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    We trace both the repeated computation and the shifted answers of current engines to one root cause, the coupling between the logical structure of a decision request and its physical execution.

  • •

    We propose Flide, which keeps each request as a tree in GPU metadata while running every round as one flat stream, and forks every state exactly with ForkAttention.

  • •

    On public hybrid and decision models, Flide answers up to an order of magnitude faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to the float32 reference in total variation.

2 Related Work

Prefix Sharing and State Branching.

Modern serving systems reduce redundant computation by caching key-value representations of reusable prompt prefixes (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2024b). Specialized execution kernels retrieve these cached representations during decoding via cascade attention (Ye et al., 2025; Juravsky et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024) or sequence-tree traversals (Yao et al., 2025). For hybrid architectures containing recurrent states (Gu and Dao, 2023; Yang et al., 2025), existing frameworks either constrain state materialization to coarse block boundaries (Pan et al., 2025; vLLM Project, 2026c; Jing et al., 2026) or require predefined checkpoint positions (Shirokikh and Nikolenko, 2026). Speculative decoding verifies token trees with tree attention (Miao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024), and its hybrid variants propagate recurrent states along the branches (Wu et al., 2025; Ghantasala, 2026; Ma, 2026). Domain-specific frontends fork requests into isolated sequences that query a shared prefix cache (Zheng et al., 2024a). However, all of these mechanisms mandate a strict temporal separation where shared prefixes must complete execution and populate memory buffers before downstream queries can consume them. Flide eliminates this decoupled caching phase by evaluating both the shared context and every branching question within a single forward pass, dynamically propagating both attention and Gated DeltaNet states across a flattened token sequence.

Decision Model Serving and Execution Exactness.

Decision-making architectures operate under strict latency budgets and rely on well-calibrated categorical distributions (TypeSafe AI, 2026; OneJev Team, 2026; Open-Jev, 2026; vLLM Semantic Router, 2026). Existing engines handle these single-token workloads either by processing questions as isolated sequences (Du et al., 2025; vLLM Project, 2026d; SGLang Project, 2026c), which repeats prefix calculations, or by concatenating candidate queries with delimiter tokens (SGLang Project, 2026a), which invalidates isolated query semantics and requires CPU-managed segmentation that breaks CUDA graph capture. Standard graph capture strategies mitigate prefill dispatch overhead by padding requests to static shapes (SGLang Team, 2026), but still treat the individual sequence as the primitive unit of execution. Even when the prefix is computed once beforehand (vLLM Project, 2026b), every question resumes from the cache as a sequence of its own. Other specialized variants incur latency penalties by scanning block masks (Chouhan and Perry, 2026; Antunes et al., 2026), packing spoken input streams into eager passes (Jin et al., 2026), or evaluating candidate trees across segmented passes (Ma et al., 2026). Compounding these systemic overheads, LLM serving engines let co-scheduled requests change the outputs of one another, whereas database systems share work across concurrent queries while keeping each query isolated (Sellis, 1988). Prefix cache substitutions create observable discrepancies compared to isolated evaluation (Patodiya, 2026), and dynamic reduction orders cause floating-point nondeterminism (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Existing batch-invariant kernels slow serving by 34 percent on Qwen3-8B in SGLang (SGLang Team, 2025), and the batch-invariant mode of vLLM cannot execute recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers (vLLM Project, 2026a). Flide resolves these scheduling and numerical conflicts simultaneously by executing multi-branch rounds through GPU-resident metadata. This approach preserves full CUDA graph replay across dynamic workloads while every answer equals its standalone computation in exact arithmetic. As summarized in Table 1, Flide is the only one of these engines that concurrently achieves single-pass execution, unpolluted query inputs, arbitrary hybrid state branching, CUDA graph replaying, and an optional bitwise-invariant mode under dynamic loads.

3 Method

As illustrated in Figure 2, Flide keeps the tree of each request as its logical structure and runs every round of requests as one flat token stream on the GPU.

3.1 Problem Formulation

A decision model receives a state and several questions about it in one request, as in the System One API (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that vLLM (vLLM Project, 2026d) and SGLang (SGLang Project, 2026c) serve. A decision request r=(s,q1,…,qn)r=(s,q_{1},\dots,q_{n}) comprises a state ss of PP tokens and nn questions, where question qiq_{i} has |qi||q_{i}| tokens, as illustrated in Figure 2(a). Flide renders the prompt for every question exactly as it would appear if asked in isolation. It defines ss as the longest sequence of leading tokens that all such prompts share before the text of their questions begins. Consequently, the concatenation s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} matches the standalone prompt for qiq_{i} token for token. Let hih_{i} denote the final hidden state at the last token of qiq_{i} when the model processes s⊕qis\oplus q_{i}. Each question qiq_{i} comes with a set of options OiO_{i}, and the engine computes the probability of each option as

pi​(o)=exp⁡(wo⊤​hi)∑o′∈Oiexp⁡(wo′⊤​hi),o∈Oi,p_{i}(o)=\frac{\exp(w_{o}^{\top}h_{i})}{\sum_{o^{\prime}\in O_{i}}\exp(w_{o^{\prime}}^{\top}h_{i})},\qquad o\in O_{i}, (1)

where wow_{o} is the row of the output head corresponding to option oo. This row belongs to a label token in a chat model or to a trained slot in a decision model. In exact arithmetic, pip_{i} depends only on ss and qiq_{i}, remaining independent of other concurrent questions or requests.

Naively processing s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} as a separate sequence for every question requires n​P+∑i|qi|nP+\sum_{i}|q_{i}| token computations, which redundantly evaluates the shared state nn times. Computing the state and each question exactly once reduces this cost to P+∑i|qi|P+\sum_{i}|q_{i}|. While prefix caching approximates this efficiency, it still forces every question to execute as an independent sequence that resumes from the cache. To reach this count, Flide computes the shared state and all of its questions jointly in a single forward pass, which raises three challenges once every answer must stay exact.

  • •

    First, every question must keep its exact standalone computation, which rules out any change to its input such as a delimiter before each question. Hybrid models make this harder, since their Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2025) compress all prior tokens into a single recurrent state and leave no attention matrix to mask.

  • •

    Second, rounds mixing requests of arbitrary numbers and lengths must run with minimal GPU launch overhead, given that a short decision request takes only a few milliseconds of GPU time. CUDA graphs remove these launches but fix the shape of every launch, whereas the tree of a round changes from one round to the next.

  • •

    Third, when a state grows incrementally over the successive steps of an agent, the engine must reuse the unchanged part of the previous state and compute only its short mutable tail and the newly appended tokens.

3.2 ForkAttention

To resolve the first challenge, ForkAttention structures each decision request as a computational tree where the shared state forms a common trunk and the questions fork as independent branches. Evaluating the shared trunk once allows every question to inherit the prefix representation without redundant computation or prompt modifications. Pointwise operations, including linear projections, normalization layers, and multilayer perceptrons, remain indifferent to this tree structure because they process each token in complete isolation. State forking therefore requires intervention only in the token-mixing layers, which must grant questions access to the shared trunk while isolating sibling branches from each other. Flide maps this tree onto the GPU by flattening an entire round of requests into a single continuous token stream without padding. State tokens appear first, followed by their corresponding question branches,

[s(1)​∣s(2)​∣⋯∣​q1(1)​∣⋯∣​qn1(1)∣​q1(2)∣⋯],\bigl[\,s^{(1)}\mid s^{(2)}\mid\cdots\mid q^{(1)}_{1}\mid\cdots\mid q^{(1)}_{n_{1}}\mid q^{(2)}_{1}\mid\cdots\bigr], (2)

where s(j)s^{(j)} denotes the state trunk of the jj-th request and qc(j)q^{(j)}_{c} denotes its cc-th question branch, as illustrated in Figure 2(b). Every token in this flattened stream carries metadata indicating its request index jj, its branch index cc (with c=0c=0 designating the trunk), and its sequential position tt. The tree thus remains the logical structure of every request, the stream is only its physical layout, and these indices map every token from one to the other. Positional indices for each question continue from PP, and the rotary embedding of any question token therefore matches the one it receives in the standalone sequence s⊕qis\oplus q_{i}. If the state incorporates images, vision encoder representations replace image placeholder tokens once per state. The state retains the native multimodal rotary positions of the model, enabling each question to resume from the position immediately following the state boundary.

3.2.1 Full-Attention Layers

A query token xx attends to a key token yy when the following conditions hold,

jy=jx,cy∈{0,cx},ty≤tx,j_{y}=j_{x},\qquad c_{y}\in\{0,c_{x}\},\qquad t_{y}\leq t_{x}, (3)

which guarantees that the key belongs to the same request, resides either in the shared state or within the query’s specific question, and does not appear later in the sequence. Each question thus attends only to its trunk and itself as in s⊕qis\oplus q_{i}, similar to the tree attention that speculative decoding applies to candidate tokens (Miao et al., 2024). A sliding-window layer of width WW, as in Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), adds tx−ty<Wt_{x}-t_{y}<W, which selects the same keys as in s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} because the positions agree.

3.2.2 Gated DeltaNet Layers

Hybrid models replace attention with Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) in most of their layers. Such a layer folds every token into a single matrix-valued recurrent state 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} of fixed size by the gated delta rule,

𝐒t\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{t} =αt​𝐒t−1​(𝐈−ηt​𝐤t​𝐤t⊤)+ηt​𝐯t​𝐤t⊤,\displaystyle=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\bigl(\mathbf{I}-\eta_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top}\bigr)+\eta_{t}\mathbf{v}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top}, (4)
𝐨t\displaystyle\mathbf{o}_{t} =𝐒t​𝐪t,\displaystyle=\mathbf{S}_{t}\mathbf{q}_{t},

where 𝐪t\mathbf{q}_{t}, 𝐤t\mathbf{k}_{t} and 𝐯t\mathbf{v}_{t} are the query, key and value vectors of token tt, and the decay αt\alpha_{t} and write strength ηt\eta_{t} are computed from the token. A short causal convolution in front of the rule further mixes each token with its few predecessors. Since 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} already contains every earlier token, a mask cannot separate two questions that share a sequence. Each question therefore has to continue the recurrence from 𝐒P\mathbf{S}_{P}, the recurrent state at the last token of ss. Flide therefore runs each Gated DeltaNet layer in two calls over the stream of Equation 2. The first call processes the state segments of all requests and outputs 𝐒P\mathbf{S}_{P} and the convolution window of each request. The second call processes the question segments of all requests at once, and each question starts from the 𝐒P\mathbf{S}_{P} of its own request through an index without copying any state. The convolution reads the predecessors of each token through the same kind of index, which lets the first tokens of a question see the last tokens of its state. Every question thus continues from the exact state its standalone input would reach, at any position and with every token computed once, as illustrated in Figure 2(b).

3.2.3 Exactness

In a causal model, where the state never attends to a question, the visibility rule of Equation 3 and the two calls of every Gated DeltaNet layer together give each question the computation of its standalone prompt.

Proposition 3.1.

For a causal model in exact arithmetic, the hidden state computed by Flide at any token of question qiq_{i} is identical to the hidden state at that token when the model processes s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} in isolation, regardless of other requests and questions in the same round.

The proof proceeds by induction over the layers and is provided in Appendix A. In other words, the result that the tree of a request defines holds under any flat layout of the round. In floating point, the differences stay at the rounding level, which the tests of Appendix G check on every change of the engine.

3.3 Flat-Graph Execution

Flat-graph execution resolves the second challenge by turning the forks of a round into GPU work with negligible launch overhead, as illustrated in Figure 2(c). A short decision request on a small model takes only a few milliseconds of GPU time, which launching several thousand kernels one by one would dominate. Although CUDA graphs eliminate these sequential launches, a captured graph fixes the shape of every kernel launch, whereas a server encounters rounds containing requests of highly variable numbers and lengths. To reconcile this, Flide keeps the tree of a round purely as GPU data. The shape of every launch then depends on the length of the flat stream alone, and a small collection of captured graphs accommodates any mix of requests and questions.

3.3.1 GPU-Resident Metadata

All variables determined by the round composition, including segment lengths, positional indices, key ranges, and state indices, reside in compact device buffers populated before graph replay, from which every kernel derives its workload. The attention kernel fetches keys from two sources, the shared state of the request and the query’s specific question, and skips the states of other requests interleaved in the stream. The kernel constructs its tile table directly on the GPU, loads the fully visible key blocks without applying a mask, and restricts masking exclusively to partially visible blocks. The Gated DeltaNet layers iterate over a list of fixed-length chunks populated by each round, with any unused entries beyond the active chunks returning immediately. Consequently, altering the mix of requests only modifies the buffer contents while preserving the exact launch configuration of the captured graph.

3.3.2 Graphs over Stream Lengths

Building on length-bucketed CUDA graph capture (SGLang Team, 2026), Flide allows rounds with different decision-tree structures to reuse the same captured graph. At server initialization, Flide captures a family of flat graphs indexed by stream capacity TT. Each graph also reserves fixed capacities for requests, question segments, Gated DeltaNet chunks, and readout rows. The actual request boundaries and question dependencies are supplied through GPU-resident metadata, allowing different request mixes to share the same execution graph. For each round, Flide selects the smallest graph whose buffers can accommodate both its flattened stream and associated metadata. Tokens are packed without padding between requests; padding occurs only at the tail, where dense layers still perform computation but no valid token accesses the padded positions. If a round exceeds the largest graph’s capacity, Flide splits it along request boundaries into multiple replays. An individual request exceeding this capacity runs through the same flat-stream execution without CUDA graph replay.

3.3.3 Selective Readout

The output head of Equation 1 reads only the last token of every question, so in the final layer every token still contributes its keys and values while the rest of the layer, its MLP included, runs only at these rows. An index buffer of fixed size in every graph holds the rows, which skips most of the final-layer work without changing any output in exact arithmetic.

3.4 Incremental State Forking

Successive steps of an agent trajectory often share most of their state, and therefore most of the trunk of their decision trees. Flide exploits this overlap by checkpointing the state of a request at an internal position mm. A later request can resume from the checkpoint when its tokens up to mm match. Each checkpoint stores the float32 recurrent state and convolution window of every Gated DeltaNet layer at mm, together with the keys and values of the full-attention layers before mm. This allows a resumed request to compute the same function as a fresh one in exact arithmetic. Flide places mm slightly before the end of a state so that tokens likely to change at the next step, such as those at the end of a conversational turn, fall after the checkpoint.

Flide generates the checkpoint during the same forward pass that computes the request’s answers. To achieve this, Flide divides the state segments of the stream into two levels at their checkpoints. Each Gated DeltaNet layer processes the two levels sequentially, saving the final states of the first level as checkpoints and passing them to the second through the same state-indexing mechanism used for question forking. For full attention, cached keys and values precede newly computed ones in a buffer representing each state’s history, allowing resumed states to be processed without occupying a contiguous span of the flat stream. At each agent step, Flide thus computes the new tokens and a short uncached tail only once for all questions, saves a checkpoint for the next step, and forks the questions from the completed state, as illustrated in Figure 2(d).

3.5 Bitwise Determinism

Proposition 3.1 makes the result of the tree independent of the flat layout in exact arithmetic, yet in floating point a matrix product over more rows may pick another kernel, tile shape or reduction split and reorder the sums of an output element (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Flide therefore offers an optional mode, in the spirit of batch-invariant inference (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), in which no reduction depends on the composition of the round. Every matrix product sums each output element in a fixed order whatever the number of rows, and every question gets attention tiles and Gated DeltaNet chunks of its own, which start its reductions exactly at the fork. A question asked alone also runs as its state and one branch in this mode, and every answer computed from a full state therefore keeps the bits of the question asked alone under any load on the same hardware and software.

4 Experiments

4.1 Settings

Workloads.

We build six workloads from four public datasets, RACE (Lai et al., 2017), QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022), MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018) and the Decision Index (Decision Index, 2026). Two of them send one question per state, with RACE passages and with QuALITY articles cut to 3,600 tokens. The other four send every question of a state in one request, as the datasets come, from four questions per RACE passage to 48 per MultiRC paragraph on average, as Table 2 lists and Appendix C details.

Baselines.

We compare against vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024a) through their decision endpoints, against SGLang’s multi-item scoring (SGLang Project, 2026a), MIS in the tables, and on the dedicated decision models against vllm-jev (mode-io, 2026) and its RadixFlow scheduler (Jing et al., 2026). vLLM, SGLang and Flide serve the instruct models of Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) from 0.8B to 27B and of Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026) from E2B to 31B, multi-item scoring the Qwen3.5 models and vllm-jev Open-Jev-2B and Open-Jev-9B (Open-Jev, 2026), all in bfloat16 with CUDA graphs on, except multi-item scoring, which turns them off. Flide and vLLM read the same prompts, while SGLang and vllm-jev render their own templates, and Appendix B lists the versions and settings of every engine.

Metrics.

Lat. is the median latency in milliseconds of a request from a single client, and C8, C32 and C64 are the requests per second under 8, 32 and 64 closed-loop clients. Against a float32 forward pass of the same model, Agr. is the share of questions with the same top answer, TV the mean total variation distance in points, P99 the 99th percentile of the largest change in one option’s probability, and Flip the share of decisions that a threshold of 0.5 takes differently. Acc. is the share of correct answers, and Stab. the share of questions whose top answer at 64 clients equals the one at a single client.

Setup.

All measurements run on one NVIDIA H200 GPU, with the engines started one after another and every prefix cache emptied before each level. Every row is sent four times, twice for DI and the full QuALITY articles, and each copy’s state starts with its own tag, which keeps any request from reusing the state of another.

4.2 Main Results

Table 3 compares the three engines on Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, while Figure 3 summarizes their relative speeds across workloads, from which we draw three findings.

First, Flide is faster even with a single question per state. On Qwen3.5, it cuts the latency of a lone request by up to 3.2 times on the smallest model. The gain comes from one flat-graph replay per round, against the heavier front ends and schedulers of generation engines. Under load, where model computation dominates, Flide matches the best baseline.

Second, the advantage grows substantially when multiple questions share a state. Flide leads at every model size and concurrency level, achieving up to 9.5 times lower latency and 8.5 times higher throughput than the best baseline. The largest gains occur on QuALITY and MultiRC, which carry the most questions per state, since ForkAttention computes the shared state once for all of them while conventional engines repeatedly compute or restore it. Multi-item scoring also shares the state but introduces delimiter tokens and runs without CUDA graphs. Flide achieves higher throughput while preserving each question’s standalone computation in exact arithmetic.

Finally, Flide also maintains its advantage on full-attention models. Even against vLLM’s prefix cache, which already computes the shared state of Gemma 4 once, Flide cuts the latency of multi-question requests by 1.1 to 2.9 times. These results highlight the efficiency of executing an entire request in one forward pass, beyond the computational savings provided by prefix caching.

4.3 Answer Fidelity

Table 4 reads the answers of the Qwen3.5 models, and averaged over the four sizes, Flide’s top answer agrees with the float32 reference most often on every workload. Flide’s accuracy stays within 1.2 points of vLLM’s in every cell, so it gains its speed at the same accuracy, and SGLang’s differs more only on MultiRC, where it words yes-or-no questions its own way. Batching changes the order of floating-point sums, so every engine changes some answers between one and 64 clients, Flide at most 0.2 percent, SGLang up to 1.7 and vLLM up to 3.2 percent. In the mode of Section 3.5, Flide returns the same bits at any load, as Appendix E shows.

4.4 In-depth Analysis

Further analyses, from identical bits and the time one request spends in each part of an engine to the start-up of a server, follow in Appendix E.

Ablation.

Table 5 removes individual components of Flide on Qwen3.5-4B to isolate their performance contributions. Without state forks, each question executes as an independent sequence, causing the latency of a multi-question QuALITY article to increase by more than an order of magnitude. Without CUDA graphs, a solitary request launches thousands of sequential kernels, yielding a severe latency penalty on short inputs. Without flat graphs, every request necessitates a distinct replay, stripping a round of short RACE requests of over one third of its throughput. Finally, selective readout delivers further throughput gains by avoiding redundant token projections across all workloads. Each component thus removes a distinct cost, from repeated state computation to kernel launches, graph replays and final-layer work, and together they give Flide its end-to-end speed.

Dedicated decision models.

Table 6 evaluates Open-Jev, the exact architecture vllm-jev and its RadixFlow scheduler were designed to serve. Flide outperforms both baselines across all configurations, achieving roughly threefold speedups on short inputs and maintaining an advantage of up to 1.7 times on long prompts where the forward pass dominates execution time. This demonstrates that a generalized engine operating over the logical request tree outpaces heavily specialized systems.

The cost of a delimiter.

Multi-item scoring shares context by inserting a delimiter token before each question, and Figure 4 illustrates the resulting penalty on Qwen3.5-4B. The median outputs of this delimiter approach diverge from the float32 reference roughly twelve times as much as those of Flide, whereas the curves of Flide, vLLM, and SGLang overlap. Across all sizes and workloads, the delimiter method flips up to 29 percent of categorical decisions, compared to a maximum of 2.3 percent for Flide, as detailed in Table 11 of Appendix E. Properly sharing the internal state thus keeps Flide closest to the float32 reference in total variation, confirming that the shifted answers of multi-item scoring stem directly from its input modifications.

Questions per state.

Figure 5a isolates a state of roughly two thousand tokens from a QuALITY article and evaluates performance across a growing number of questions. Because vLLM and SGLang process each question as an independent sequence, their latencies increase drastically as the questions grow. Flide computes the shared state exactly once and only appends the tokens specific to each branch. With 64 questions on the state, Flide operates 12.7 times faster than vLLM and maintains a substantial lead over SGLang. This follows the cost analysis of Section 3.1, as the stream grows only by the tokens of each question, while separate sequences repeat the whole state for every question.

States that grow.

We replay dozens of SWE-agent trajectories (Yang et al., 2024) from a public dataset (Nebius, 2024), truncating them after their initial steps to yield over a thousand total states, and pose multiple questions against the complete history at every turn. As Table 7 and Figure 5b illustrate, the marginal latency cost per thousand tokens on Flide stays around one millisecond. In contrast, vLLM and SGLang suffer an order of magnitude higher latency penalty by running each question independently, while multi-item scoring degrades severely by recomputing the entire history at every step. Regardless of the agent count, Flide ultimately completes 4.4 to 7.2 times the steps per second of the strongest baseline.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine for decision models that decouples the logical tree structure of each request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. By leveraging ForkAttention, Flide forks intermediate states precisely across both attention and recurrent layers, replaying arbitrary execution rounds through compact pre-recorded graphs while extending agent histories directly from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. This architecture resolves the fundamental conflict between hierarchical request logic and sequential token execution, eliminating both the redundant prefix computations and the delimiter tokens that shift the answers of existing serving engines. Extensive evaluations across hybrid and full-attention architectures, specialized decision benchmarks, and real-world agent trajectories demonstrate that Flide achieves substantial speedups over current state-of-the-art frameworks while staying closest to the float32 reference distributions on Qwen3.5. By unifying high-throughput parallel execution with strict mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in next-generation LLM agent systems.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 3.1

Fix a request with state ss of PP tokens and a question qiq_{i}. Every token of s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} enters the stream with the token id and position it has in the standalone sequence, and norms, projections, the MLP and the rotary embedding act on one token at a time. A full-attention layer lets each token of qiq_{i} see exactly the tokens before it in s⊕qis\oplus q_{i} by Equation 3, and each Gated DeltaNet layer continues qiq_{i} from the recurrent state 𝐒P\mathbf{S}_{P} and the convolution window that ss reaches alone. Equal inputs to a layer therefore give equal outputs, and induction over the layers proves the proposition, since no step involves another request or question of the round. A checkpoint restores the values that a fresh pass reaches at its position, and selective readout only drops rows that no read uses, so both keep this equality.

Appendix B Engine Versions and Launch Settings

Table 8 lists the engines, and every cell of vLLM reports the faster of its two builds, while the analyses and the comparisons on growing states, repeated states and images run the build of 14 October. SGLang and vllm-jev use their own prompt formats, and multi-item scoring receives the state as the query and every question as an item, as the token ids that Flide and vLLM read. The token-id rows of Table 13 send the same ids to the completion endpoint of vLLM and to the score endpoint of SGLang without multi-item scoring. For the images of GQA, vLLM and SGLang serve their chat endpoints with one request per question, thinking off and one output token, and a label outside the 20 most likely tokens counts as zero. The float32 reference runs with TF32 disabled, a threshold of 0.5 acts when the probability of yes or of the top option reaches it, and the client sends 32 warm-up requests before each level.

Appendix C Workload Construction

Table 2 lists the six workloads as the engines receive them, built from public sets by scripts in the release with a fixed seed. Its token counts come from the tokenizer of Qwen3.5, and those of the Gemma 4 tokenizers stay within 8 percent of them. RACE samples 256 questions of the middle-school test set of RACE with their passages (Lai et al., 2017), and RACE all samples 256 passages of the same set with all of their questions. QuALITY samples 256 questions of the validation set of QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) and cuts each article at a line boundary so that the article, the question and its longest option fit 3,600 tokens with room for the template, inside the 4,096-token context of the Open-Jev models, while QuALITY all keeps all 115 validation articles at full length with all of their questions. The comparison with vllm-jev runs its two Open-Jev models on RACE and on this cut QuALITY. MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018) turns every candidate answer of a question into the yes-or-no question question Is “answer” a correct answer?, adding whole questions to a paragraph while it holds at most 64. DI samples 760 requests of the public set of the Decision Index (Decision Index, 2026), and 81 of them hold a choice question with more than 26 options, more letters than the alphabet holds, so 679 requests with 3,510 choice and 125 yes-or-no questions remain, 2,422 of them with a gold answer. Every engine reads at most 26 options per choice question, 10 levels per score question and 64 questions per request, and every other workload satisfies these limits as built. In the cold setting each copy of a row begins its state with a line naming the copy and the row, so no request shares a prompt prefix with another, while the questions of one request still share their state on every engine.

Flide and vLLM render a question as vLLM’s decision endpoint renders it for chat models, one user turn with the state, a blank line and the question, followed by the opening of the assistant turn with thinking turned off, as shown in Figure 6. The answer is the distribution of the next token over the labels of the options, renormalized over those labels. In Flide the part of the prompt before the question is the state of the stream and every question with the rest of the prompt is a branch, so its tokens are exactly those of vLLM’s prompt. SGLang writes structured states as compact JSON and opens a yes-or-no question with Is the following true? followed by the question, listing only the outcomes that carry a description, and the reference for SGLang is computed in this wording.

Appendix D Full Results

Figures 7 and 8 follow Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma 4 E4B from one to 64 clients. Tables 9 and 10 list every level of each engine on every workload for Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma 4 E4B, where multi-item scoring serves only the Qwen3.5 workloads with every question of a state in one request, with the median and 99th percentile latency and the throughput. With more than one question per request, Flide keeps the lowest 99th percentile latency at every number of clients on both models, which extends Table 3 to the tail.

Appendix E Further Analysis

A growing state.

Figure 5b follows the step latency of Section 4.4 on Qwen3.5-4B over the full range of history lengths, with one agent and with eight. Every engine keeps its cache on except multi-item scoring, whose launch settings turn its radix cache off, and each agent sends its next step once the last one is answered.

Identical bits.

With the batch-invariant mode of Section 3.5, every answer in Table 12 keeps its bits at any load on all six models and six workloads. On each Qwen3.5 model, every forked answer also has the bits of its question asked alone, on all 626 questions of DI, RACE, MultiRC and QuALITY. The invariant mode costs at most 10 percent of the throughput at 64 clients, against the 34 percent that the batch-invariant kernels of SGLang lose on Qwen3-8B (SGLang Team, 2025).

Where the time goes.

In Table 13, which takes one request on the 0.8B model apart, vLLM fed token ids computes the same tokens on QuALITY and MultiRC as behind its endpoint. The 187 ms it loses on a QuALITY article and the 57 ms on a MultiRC paragraph thus go to rendering and tokenizing the prompt of every question. Below their front ends vLLM and SGLang still compute 1.5 to 6.5 times the tokens of Flide, since every question carries its own copy of the state and a prefix cache restores only part of it. SGLang’s multi-item scoring computes the tokens of Flide to within two percent, one delimiter per question, yet at every size it takes longer for a request alone, up to 8.0 times on the 0.8B model, and serves 1.1 to 4.0 times fewer requests at 64 clients, as it runs without CUDA graphs and builds the metadata of its Gated DeltaNet branches on the CPU.

Memory and GPU time.

On Qwen3.5-4B in Table 14, which runs the vLLM build of 14 October, vLLM and SGLang reserve most of the card for their key and value caches by default, and their peak follows a setting. Flide holds 18.8 GiB at its peak, the model, 2.1 GiB of CUDA graphs and the work space of its largest rounds. At 64 clients on DI every engine keeps a kernel running 71 to 91 percent of the time, yet Flide turns that time into 68 thousand useful tokens per second against 32 to 46 thousand for the others, since vLLM and SGLang spend part of it on states that they compute again for each question and multi-item scoring runs its kernels without CUDA graphs. Busy time thus measures how full the GPU is, and useful tokens measure how much of that work a decision needed. Held to a tenth of the card, vLLM and SGLang peak at 17.2 and 18.7 GiB, close to Flide, and Flide’s lead holds at equal memory.

The lead under load.

As shown in Figure 9, the lead of Flide changes with the number of clients. With few clients the GPU waits for the engine, and removing launches and scheduling rounds pays off on every workload. With many clients the single-question workloads become bound by the forward pass, which every engine computes in about the same time, and Flide still leads on QuALITY by about four percent. On DI the lead persists at every level, because computing each state once saves GPU work as well as overhead.

Questions about images.

Qwen3.5 reads images as well, and an agent that acts on a screen asks its questions about what it sees. We take the 397 images of the balanced test-dev split of GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) with their 4,525 yes-or-no questions, eleven per image on average, and send each image with all of its questions as one request. This comparison runs the vLLM build of 14 October, whose decision endpoint takes no images for these models, and SGLang’s endpoint takes none either, so both answer through their chat endpoints with one request per question, the image first and the label probabilities read from the first output token. As Table 15 shows, Flide answers an image 5.0 to 7.5 times faster than the better of the two alone and serves 3.1 to 5.4 times its requests at 64 clients, while its answers stay closest to the float32 reference on every model and all three engines stay within half a point of the reference’s accuracy of 70.4, 77.7 and 79.3 percent.

Start-up.

A Triton kernel is compiled on first use, and its tuning runs on first use as well, so an engine built on Triton can spend minutes before its first answer. Flide ships its kernels compiled and tuned in a bundle independent of the Triton installation. As Table 17 shows, a 0.8B server answers its first request after about 35 s with the bundle against 181 s without it, since the bundle brings every kernel compiled and tuned, and its answers are identical bit for bit.

Appendix F Recurring States

Table 16 sends every row once with every engine’s cache on, Flide’s saved states and the prefix caches of vLLM and SGLang, so a state that recurs can be served from the cache. On the 4B model Flide answers a recurring QuALITY article in 18.4 ms against 39.1 ms for vLLM and 75.0 ms for SGLang, because it resumes from the saved recurrent state without recomputing a block. Flide stays ahead in every cell, by 2.6 to 44 percent under load on the single-question workloads and by 1.6 to 2.1 times on DI.

Appendix G Correctness Tests

Every change to the engine passes a ladder of tests before any speed is measured. The kernel tests compare the attention and fused pointwise kernels with a PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) reference over head sizes, grouped heads, sliding windows and every layout of a round, where every error stays at the rounding level of float32 and bfloat16 and the key blocks read without a mask return the same bits as with one. The forward tests run OneJev1.5-0.8B (OneJev Team, 2026) in float32 on ten requests of DI (Decision Index, 2026) against a float64 forward pass, where the transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) reaches a largest error of 6.0×10−36.0\times 10^{-3} and every change of Flide must stay within twice that error. Flide’s eager forward and its CUDA graphs, requests replayed together in one flat graph, requests with images and videos and requests resumed from a saved state all stay within this bound, while a request replayed after a different one and a server with two front-end processes return the same results as before.

Appendix H Supported Models

Table 18 lists the decision models that Flide serves, each against its release engine on the first 32 requests of RACE, MultiRC and QuALITY, of a 760-request sample of the Decision Index and of GQA with images. Both mammoth and elephant read each block both ways in their full-attention layers, and since their state never reads a question, their questions still fork it under the rule of Section 3.2 without ty≤txt_{y}\leq t_{x}. Jeffan, StartLux and Lychee read the whole prompt of each question both ways, so every question runs as a sequence of its own in the stream, and pplx-decider reads all questions of a request in one sequence. Intern-Decision reads at most 16 questions a request, so its cells keep the requests within that limit among the first 32. The Open-Jev row repeats RACE and QuALITY of Table 6, all 256 requests against the better setting of vllm-jev, and adds DI and MultiRC on their first 32 requests against the same setting. The OneJev row compares OneJev1.5-0.8B with qev, the engine it ran on before Flide, on all 760 requests of the DI sample and the first 32 of MultiRC and QuALITY. Models built on Qwen3.8, which shares the architecture of Qwen3.5, appear in the table with a Qwen3.5 backbone.
